This  edition  was  begun  in  1855.  ^  some  of  tlie  collations  liaving

Without  under-rating  the  first  and  second  objects,  it  was  the 
third  which  principally  guided  this  effort. 

The  early  rites  of  the  Western  Church  are  known  from  frag- 
mentary  materials  of  various  dates  and  incidental  references  in 
the  Fathers,  and  it  is  not  easy  to  make  out  the 
evidence  for  the  early  existence  of  particular  rites        Evidence      of 
and  ceremonies.     The  Roman  Service  Books  have     imperfect. 
been  altered  since  the  Reformation ;  and,  without 
impugning  the  good  intentions  and  good  faith  of  those  who  altered 
them,  it  may  at  least  be  permitted  to  us  to  study  the  unaltered 
forms  which  were  in  use  here  in  our  own  country,  and  which  are 
naturally  most  akin  to  our  Prayer  Book,  and  to  learn  what  we  can 
of  the  modes  of  worship  of  our  forefathers,  and  of  those  who  lived 
in  the  earliest  days  of  the  Church,  in  the  books  of  this  country, 
rather  than  from  books  which  contain  the  traditions  of  foreign 
lands.

Every  Cathedral  had  its  customs,  going  back  to  its  origin,  and 
rcpresenting  what  the  first  Missionaries  brought  with  them,  but 
altered  from  time  to  time  as  reverence  seemed  to  demand  new  rites; 
while  otlier  rites,  such  as  Communion  in  both  kinds  in  the  Service 
by  the  whole  congregation,  fell  out  of  use.  In  each  case,  the 
bulk  of  the  observances  would  be  old  ;  the  new  matter — new  in 
comparison  with  the  previous  code — woukl  probably  be  the  customs 
that  had  grown  up,  and  which  it  was  thought  desirable  to  perpetu- 
ate.  Many  things  were  changed  as  the  Church  grew  in  wealth ;

It  may  be  that  tlie  changes  made  by  S.  Osmund  were  great. 
The  time  was  one  of  change.  Foreign  Ecclesiastics  for  some  time 
before  the  Conquest  had  brought  foreign  rites  into  England,  and 
that  event  was  likely  to  increase  the  tendency  to  put  aside  English 
customs.  Still,  it  is  probable,  that  the  larger  part  of  the  Missal 
was  not  changed.  It  does  not  seem  to  have  been  held  that — 
whatever  may  have  happened  as  to  peculiar  rites  which  may  have 
been  derived  from  the  British  Church — the  English  Missal  was 
ever  other  than  Roman  ; '  and  what  we  know  of  the  Durham  Ritual, 
S.  Dunstan's  reforms,  and  the  books  of  Leofric  Bishop  of  Exeter, 
tends  upon  the  whole  in  the  same  direction. 

The  statement,  then,  that  S.  Osmund  established  the  Use  of 
Sarum,  answers  no  question,  and  we  still  have  to  enquire  in  detail, 
liow  much  had  been  always  used  by  the  English  Church,  and  when 
and  from  what  quarters  the  changes  came  1

purpose  of  those  who  w^ished  to  revive  forgotten  rites  than  to  be 
so  opposed. 

The  doctrine  of  the  Eucharist,  and  the  changes  of  view  about  it, 
must  always  be  matter  of  interesting  historical  study,  and  cannot 
be  dissociated  from  the  externals  connected  with  it  and  the  rest 
of  Divine  Service.  The  studies  and  the  necessities  of  the  times 
have  brought  these  things  of  intrinsically  less  importance  into 
great  prominence.  With  the  revival  of  Eucharistic  vestments, 
whatever  interpretation  is  put  on  the  Ornaments  Rubric,  whether 
the  vestments  prescribed  by  the  Rubric  of  the  first  Prayer  Book  of 
Edward  VI.  are  obligatory,  or  w^e  have  to  substitute  for  them  in 
Ciithedral  and  Collegiate  Churches  Copes  for  the  Celebrant  and  the 
Gospeller  and  Epistler  at  all  solemn  celebrations  of  Holy  Com- 
munion,  the  Chasubles  or  Copes  will  have  to  be  made  to  agree  with 
the  rules  for  Altar  Cloths,  which  have  now  for  many  years  been 
attended  to  with  more  or  less  of  Ritual  accuracy,  and  in  the  end  it 
is  probable  that  the  ancient  rulcs  of  colour  of  each  Diocese  will  be 
adopted.

Mode  of  Nara-  The  editions  are  designated  by  the  year  of  publi- 
ingEditions.  cation ;  "87"  meaning  the  edition  of  1487;  *'34" 

that  of  1534,  and  so  forth.  When  more  than  one 
edition  was  printed  in  the  same  year,  they  are  distinguished  by 
the  initial  of  the  place  of  publication  placed  after  the  date ;  and 
when  there  is  ambiguity  also  as  to  the  place,  the  initial  of  one  of 
the  printers  or  publishers  foUows ;  where  no  name  of  place  occurs, 
the  initial  of  the  printer  is  given.  Thus,  the  edition  printed  in 
1527  at  Paris  by  Prevost  is  represented  by  27PP.;  that  printed  by 
Regnault  by  27PR.;  and  editions  of  the  same  year,  printed  at  Ant- 
werp,  and  by  Byrkman  with  no  designation  of  phace,  by  27A.  and 
27B.  At  the  end  of  the  copy  of  the  last  mentioned  edition,  which 
is  in  the  British  Museum,  occur  a  few  leaves  of  a  ditFerent  edition, 
which  have  been  designated  for  convenience  271. 

When  an  edition  bears  two  dates,  it  is  denoted  by  a  fraction. 
The  edition  begun  in  1510  and  ended  in  1511  is  denoted  by  -  :  so 
likewise  -'  denotes  the  edition  printed  in  1554  and  1555. 

M54.  denotes  the  Sarum  Manual  of  that  year;  P  with  a  figure 
following  it,  is  the  Sarum  Processional  of  the  year  indicated ;  and 
B56.  is  the  small  Breviary  of  that  year,  printed  at  Paris. 

Before  this  edition  was  begun,  a  comparison  of  editions  w^as  made, 
sufficient  to  show  a  probable  division  into  four  or  five  Classes,  and 
some  minor  subdivisions.  In  the  Notes,  only  one 
edition  of  each  Class  has  been  mentioned,  except 
when  it  was  observed  that  one  edition  differed  from 
others  of  the  same  Chiss.

The  measurements  were  taken  by  marking  on  the  top  and  the

of  the  Canon  that  had  been  measured,  with  the  number  of  lines 
in  each.  It  was  soon  found  that  not  only  the  book  itself  and  the 
Canon  differed  in  size,  but  that  the  pages  themselves  were  not 
aUvays  of  the  same  number  of  lines.  Whether  this  is  original  or 
has  been  caused  by  ingenious  contrivances  for  making  copies  per- 
fect — or  seemingly  perfect,  by  putting  togother  leaves  of  different 
editions — is  a  niatter  which  need  not  be  considered  now,  though 
it  may  be  well  to  mention  that  in  some  of  the  copies  that  have 
been  long  in  the  Bodleian,  gaps  have  been  filled  up  with  leaves 
very  much  smaller  than  those  of  the  imperfect  editions.  It  is 
possible  also  that  Canons  of  other  editions  —  some  possibly  not 
of  English  Uses— may  have  been  inserted  in  copies  of  the  Sarum 
MissaL 

The  numbers  of  inches  in  the  measures  noted  have  becn  marked 
since.     Some  of  the  nieasures  have  been  taken  bv  friends  where  the 


X\ll  IMUOFACE. 

copies  wcre  not  accessible.  Where  tlie  memoranda  of  measurement 
are  founJ  to  ditfer,  they  are  given  as  tliey  are  without  attemj)t  to 
make  them  agree. 

The  rule  followed  about  marks  to  indicate  editions  is  this  : — The 
century  is  left  out,  as  that  cau  lead  to  no  ambiguity.  If  there  are 
more  editions  than  one  of  the  same  date,  the  initial  of  the  place  is 
added, — L.  London,  R.  Rouen,  P.  Paris,  A.  Antwerp  ;  *  and  when 
tliere  are  several  editions  printed  the  same  year  at  Paris  or  Rouen, 
the  initial  of  some  printer  or  publislier  is  added.  In  a  few  cases 
where  the  place  is  not  given,  the  initial  of  the  printer's  name  fol- 
lows  the  date, 

The  Missals  arranged  in  order  of  the  Size  of  the  Page  are  given 
in  Appendix  II. 

Appendix  III.  gives  the  Classes. 

It  has  been  thought  wcll  in  Appendix  IV.  to  give  these  figures 
over  again,  along  with  the  number  of  leaves  in  each  part,  or  at 
least  an  approximation  to  a  correct  statement  of  them. 

When  there  are  but  three  numbers  they  indicate  the  Temporale, 
Sanctorale,  and  the  Commune ;  and,  when  possible,  the  first  is 
divided  into  thrce — the  first  up  to  Easter.  and  the  two  others  the 
rest  of  the  Teniporale  and  the  Canon. 

In  D.  and  the  later  editions  the  insertion  of  other  matter  before 
and  after  the  Canon  necessitates  three  figures. 

The  difFerent  arrangement  of  the  editions  makes  accuracy  diffi- 
cult,  because  the  Canon  in  the  oldest  and  best  editions  is  placed  at 
Easter,  and  in  the  greater  number  of  the  later  editions  after  the 
end  of  the  Temporale,  as  it  is  given  here,  while  several  pages  of 
prayers  occur  where  it  seems  to  have  pleased  the  Printer  to  put 
them.  It  was  soon  found  that  the  carelessness  of  pagination  was 
so  great,  that  nothing  could  be  done  with  certainty  unless  each 
edition  was  colhited  througliout.  This  also  has  been  done  in  many 
cases,  but  it  is  feared  that  in  work  extending  over  20  or  oO  years 
errors  may  be  detected.

Many  books,  when  Printing  had  hitely  been  introduced,  liad  no 
Title-page,  the  particuhirs  of  place  and  date  being  given  at  the  end, 
in  ^vhat  is  called  the  Colophon.  It  is  not  easy  always  to  find  out 
whether  a  book  has  liad  a  Title-page  or  not.  The  most  likely  place 
for  imperfections  is  the  beginning,  and  whcn  no  Title-page  appears 
it  is  necessary  to  count  the  leaves,  which  make  up  what  is  called 
here  the  first  "sheet;"  and  if  the  number  of  the  leaves  be  odd, 
and  no  leaf  missing  at  the  end  of  the  sheet,  we  may  be  sure  that 
there  was  a  Title-page. 

All  or  nearly  all  the  Missals  had  a  Title-page,  and  we  begin 
with  what  is  on  the  back  of  it,  and  then  give  what  follows — if 
tliere  be  anything — before  the  Ccilendar,  then  what  follows  between 
the  Calendar  and  the  Temporale,  and  so  on  for  the  rest;  the  object 
here  being  to  note  the  variable  parts  of  those  books,  and  to  dis- 
tinguish  them  from  the  comparatively  invariable  part — the  Calcn- 
dar,  Temporale  (including  the  Ordinary  and  Canon),  Sanctorale 
and  Commune  Sanctorum,  all  which  were  substantially  the  same 
throughout  Western  Christendom,  but  were  varied  in  details  ac- 
cording  to  the  characteristic  difFerences  of  national  and  local 
Churches. 

One  source  of  difficulty  and  error  is  the  very  im- 
perfect  state  of  preservation  of  some  of  the  books.  Materials   im- 

Some  things,  such  as  the  Canon  and  the  Pictures  perfect. 
before  it,  are  not  given  with  the  completeness  that 
might  be  wished,  because  the  copies  consulted  were  defective,  and 
in  a  first  attempt  it  is  not  necessary  to  go  elsewhere  for  more  per- 
fect  coples,  or  to  calculate  what  they  must  have  contained  from 
comparison  of  these  editions  with  other  editions.  It  generally 
happens  that  the  most  characteristic  parts — the  beginning  and  the 
end  of  the  book  and  the  Pictures,  sometimes  the  whole  Canon — 
have  been  destroyed  through  curiosity,  spitc,  or  neglect. 

This  first  attempt  to  classify  the  Contents  of  the  Sarum  Missal 
is  a  matter  of  some  difficulty  and  a  o^ood  deal  of  anxiety. 

It  has  been  made  at  different  times,  extending  ovcr  more  tlian 
30  years,  and  the  marks  used  at  first  to  discriminate  editions 
were  found  not  to  suit,  and  had  to  be  altcrcd.

The  other  editions  seem  to  have  nothing  between  Sanctorale  and 
Commune. 

The  variations  of  the  Commune  are  not  important  for  the  purpose 
of  classification,  until  the  end  ^f  the  Trigintale  Beati  Gregorii 
(col.  883*).  After  vvhich  editions  differ,  and  their  differences  are, 
perhaps,  of  more  value  than  other  differences  for  the  purpose  of 
classification. 

In  the  earlier  editions  (87.,  92.,  H.)  the  Rubric  of  the  Kyries  and 
the  Kyries  foUow  the  Trigintale  Beati  Gregorii,  and  then  the  Mass 
of  Pope  Clement.  In  94q.  they  are  transposed,  and  the  later  edi- 
tions  seem  to  divide  themselves  accordingly  into  tvvo  Uirger  divi- 
sions,  new  matter  being  added  either  at  the  end  or  between  the 
parts.  The  editions  which  follow  94q.,  and  in  which  the  Rubric 
of  the  Kyries  and  the  Kyries  are  not  given  here,  are  the  more 
numerous,  consisting  of  98.  (a  very  remarkable  edition),  2.,  and  of 
Classes  A  and  D,  in  which  last  Class  the  Dies  Irse  is  inserted  be- 
fore  the  Mass  of  Pope  Clement. 

A  and  D  are  the  most  important  Classes.  After  one  or  tvvo  of 
the  earliest  editions,  they  contain  the  editions  vvhich  are  of  the 
greatest  importance  as  to  the  Text ;  they  are  the  iiiost  numerous  as 
to  copies,  and  comprise  the  most  sumptuous  editions. 

The  Printers'  changes  of  the  editions,  vvhich  secm  to  have  bcen

derived  from  one  of  those  in  whicb  thc  Rubric  of  Kyries  followed 
immediately  the  Trigintale  Sancti  Gregorii,  are  more  complicated. 

In  some  editions  the  Kyries  seem  to  have  been  forgotten,  and  do 
not  follow  the  Riibric  concerning  them,  and  are  not  given  at  all. 
In  others,  again,  this  fault  was  noticed  and  corrected,  the  Ilubric 
and  Kyries  being  given  afterwards,  the  Rubric  twice.  This,  again, 
has  been  corrected,  by  very  properly  leaving  it  out  when  it  occurs 
first. 

After  some  consideration  and  modifications  of  plan,  it  has  been 
thought  best  to  give  the  earlier  editions  without  much  attempt  at 
combination.

For  thc  sake  of  clearness  of  arrangement,  those  variations  of  edi-

copies,  nor  yet  to  divide  them,  and  put  some  in  one  place  and  some 
in  the  other.

TABLES   AND   CALENDAR. 


Cbiitain  Tables  and  Memoranda  are  printed  in  different  editions 
on  the  back  of  the  Title  page.  They  are  apparently  information 
given  by  the  printer,  as  it  occurred  to  him,  for  the  purpose  of  filling 
up  blank  space. 

The  reverse  of  Title  is  blank  in  most  of  the  early  editions,  and 
in  19PR.  and  57,  in  which  last  the  Extracta  e  Compoto  are  placed 
on  the  last  two  pages,  ending  with  the  short  Colophon. 

In  the  Prayer  Book  of  1636,  some  Tables  are  before,  some  after 
the  Calendar,  and  there  is  a  direction  in  the  Prayer  Book  lately 
photographed — which  gives  the  alterations  agreed  on  as  in  1661 
of  this  Prayer  Book  of  1636 — to  have  them  all  placed  before  th 
Calendar  in  the  Prayer  Book  of  1662. 

They  are  now  all  after  it,  because  so  placed  in  the  Schedule  of 
the  Act  24,  Geo.  II.  c.  23,  which  gives  the  Calendar  and  the  new 
Tables,  from  which  our  ordinary  Prayer  Books  appear  to  be  copied 
correctly,  except  that  the  classical  computation  of  the  days  of  the 
month  is  omitted. 

The  Tables  and  Memoranda  in  the  Missals  appear  to  be  of  4 
classes. 

The  First,  Tabula  ad  Inveniendum  Pascha  in  Perpetuum. 
The  Second,  Tabula  ad  Inveniendum  Omnia  Festa  Mobilia. 
The  Third  document  is  called  Extracta  e  Compoto,  and  must  be 
distinguished  from 

The  Fourth,  Quoedam  Regulse  Secundum  Parvum  Compotura 
Ecclesise  Romanoe,  which  is  a  series  of  memoriae  technicse,  and  is 
printed  in  2. 

To  begin  with  the  first,  that  in  8RM.  and  other  editions. 
This  Table  agrees  with  "To  find  Easter  for  ever"  in  the  Prayer 
Book  lately  photographed.     The  Table  is  adopted  without  change, 
but  not  per  incuriam,  for  there  is  a  correction,  and  some  words  are 
added  to  the  Rubric  below. 

a 


Z^*  TABLES    AND    CALCNDAK. 

The  corresponding  Table  in  the  present  Praycr  Book  has  been 
altered  to  agree  with  the  correction  of  the  Calendar,  raade  by  the 
Act  just  mentioned. 

Tlie  Primes.  as  they  are  called  in  the  present  Table,  are  the 
Golden  Numbers,  from  I.  to  XIX.,  which  shew  the  days  of  New 
Moon  for  each  year  of  the  cycle  of  19  years,  after  which  the  changes 
of  the  Moon  recur  again  in  the  same  order. 

It  is  stated  in  Wlieatley — ed.  of  1729 — that  the  cycle  of  19  years, 
or  6940  days,  is  too  long  by  1  hour  27  minutes  and  32  seconds,  and 
that  in  consequence  the  Golden  Numbers  would  be  wrong  after  312 
years,  and  it  is  conceived  would  all  be  shifted  a  day ;  but  as  the 
intervening  New  Moons  occur  at  different  times  of  the  day,  some 
would  be  shifted  sooner  and  some  later,  and  the  cycle  lose  its  accu- 
racy  in  a  smaller  number  of  years. 

These  numbers,  then,  which  are  those  placed  at  the  edge  of  the 
Calendar,  ought  to  be  altered  continually,  though  they  probably 
stand  now  as  they  did  in  the  time  of  Durandus.  They  are  the  same 
in  the  Missals  of  13,  55P.  and  57,  but  are  not  the  same  in  the  Prayer 
Book  of  1636,  and  are  again  altered  in  the  margin  of  that  Prayer 
Book  for  the  Prayer  Book  of  1662.  The  present  Calendar,  pre- 
scribed  in  the  Act  of  Geo.  11. ,  omits  them  as  directed  by  clause  3. 

They  occur,  however,  in  the  Table  "  To  find  Easter  Day  from  the 
present  time  till  the  year  1899  inclusive,  according  to  the  foregoing 
Calendar,"  and  are  accordingly  printed  in  our  Prayer  Books ;  but 
it  is  submitted  that  the  Golden  Numbers  must  now  be  wrong,  and 
the  Table  incorrect,  and  be  altogether  useless  and  misleading.

This  third  Table,  or  rather  Statement,  is  probably  the  latest, 
and  adopted  in  the  largest  number  of  editions. 

It  is  taken  from  55P.  and  is  called  Extracta  e  Compoto. 

The  first  part,  the  same  as  that  printed  above,  is  called  the  Cycle 
of  28  years,  but  it  is  not  properly  a  cycle,  and  is  merely  what  is 
stated  here,  to  show  that  after  28  years  the  Sunday  Letter  recurs 
to  the  same  day  of  the  week,  because  the  number  28  equals  4  for 
the  Leap  years  multiplied  by  7  for  the  weeks.

^  One  of  the  chief  puzzlcs  in  history  comes  of  the  different  times  at  which  the  year 
was  supposed  to  begin.  The  most  common  ecclesiastical  custom  was  to  make  it 
begin  at  Lady-Day  or  at  liuster;  and  this  latter  time  givesan  additional  importance 
to  the  time  of  Easter,  and  the  necessity  to  be  accurate  about  it. 

In  thesc  days  of  printing  and  alraanacs  we  do  not  see  the  difficulties  of  the  Clergy 
of  old  concerning  the  time  of  Easter,  on  which  the  Moveable  Feasts  depend. 

Each  Dioccse  must  have  acted  independently,  and  Priests  far  away  from  others 
would  be  left  to  their  own  resources. 

When  Easter  was  late  in  one  year,  there  would  be  no  difficulty  about  Easter  in 
the  next,  as  the  lunar  year  of  twelve  months  is  about  eleven  days  shorter  than  the 
ordinary  solar  year,  the  Full  Moon  next  after  Lady-Day  would  go  back  eleven  days, 
and  the  Sunday  following  would  also  go  back  one  week  or  two ;  and  in  the  second 
year  Easter  would  usually  go  back  three  weeks.  In  the  third  year  Easter  would 
again  be  late,  and  this  year  would  consist  of  thirteen  lunar  months,  and  the  addi- 
tion  is  called  Embolismus.  In  the  Cycle  of  19  years,  seven  of  these  months  have  to 
be  added. 

Verses  are  given  in  Durandus  to  help  memory  of  the  places  of  these  seven  yeara 
among  the  others,  and  of  the  places  where  the  month  is  inserted  in  each  year. 

The  account  of  the  lunar  year  is  given  clearly  by  Durandus : — 

Annus  lunaris  dicitur  tribus  modis  Primo  modo  annus  lunaris  est  spacium  quo 
luna  circuit  totum  Zodiacum  quod  facit  in  viginti  septem  diebus  et  novem  horis.  Se- 
cundo  modo  dicitur  annus  lunaris  spacium  quo  luna  circtiit  solem  ab  una  ascensione 
usque  ad  aliam  et  hoc  facit  in  29  diebus  et  12  horis.  Nam  cum  luna  separatur  a  sole 
ad  peragrandum  Zodincum  et  postea  revertitur  ad  eundem  punctum  in  quo  demiserat 
solem  non  invenit  illum  ibi.  Quia  sol  jam  tantum  processit  suo  motu  quod  luna 
laborat  recurrere  ad  eum  t>ive  attingere  ipsum  duobus  diebus  et  tribus  horis.  Tertio 
dicitur  annus  lunaris  spatium  duodecim  lunationum  in  anno  commuui  et  tredecim 
in  embolismali  de  quibus  infra  dicetur. 

Embolismalis,  &c.  probably  means  that  the  month  inserted  is  even,  being  always 
of  30  days. 

Impare  par  impar.  Durandus: — Luna  paris  mensis  nunquam  trigesima  fiet. 
The  even  lunar  months — Fcbruary,  April,  &c. — were  never  of  30  days,  but  of  29, 
exoept  February  in  Leap  Year ;  and  likewise  the  odd  months  were  generally  of 
30  days,  the  odd  twelve  hours  being  supposed  to  be  always  added  to  the  carlier 
month.     Ilence,  probably,  the  meaning  of  Imparo,  kc.

The  Ilystoriao  relntc  to  the  rcaclinfr  of  lloly  Scripture  in  the  Autumn  at  the 
Breviary  Service,  and  record  the  ancient  rule  of  the  Church,  which  had  been  de- 
parted  froni  in  practice,  as  Iloly  Scripture  was  gradually  excluded  by  the  multi- 
plication  of  Saints'  Days. 

Below  the  Calendar  in  the  months  from  June  to  October  are  words  which  indicate 
the  contents  of  the  Ilystoriaa  and  tho  words  by  which  they  are  knovvn. 

The  first  for  June  is : — Post  personas  tres  librum  lleguni  dare  debes.  After  the 
Feast  of  Iloly  Trinity  the  First  Book  of  Kings  (First  Book  of  Samuel  in  our  Bible,) 
is  to  be  read,  and  then  follow  the  words  Deus  Omnium. 

The  First  Lesson  at  Matins  for  the  First  Sunday  after  Trinity  is  the  first  chapter 
ofthe  First  of  SamueJ,  and  then  follows  the  Responsory,  Deus  Omniam  exauditor 
est,  et  ipse  misit  angelum  suum,  et  tulit  me  de  ovibus  patris  mei,  et  unxit  me  unc- 
tione  misericordiae  suos. 

Versics.  Dominus  qui  eripuit  me  do  ore  leonis,  et  de  manu  bestise,  liberavit  me 
et  unxit  (me  unctione  miscricordice  suae). 

Tiie  Breviary  gives  six  Aveeks  for  to  read  the  four  Books  of  Kings,  verse  "India," 
&c.,  three;  and  so  on  with  the  others. 

In  Principio  is  the  beautiful  Anthem  on  Wisdom,  following  the  first  worda  of 
Ecclesiasticus.  Ilere  the  Breviary  gives  three  weeks  and  the  verse  "India  dat,"  &c. 
but  one. 

Then  follows  Job  with  the  Responsory  from  his  words,  Job  ii.  10  and  i.  21,  22. 
Ilere  the  Breviary  gives  one  week  and  the  Verse  two.

At  the  end  of  October  Ezekiel,  Vidi.  The  Breviary  gives  three  weeks  and  the 
Verse  two. 

The  rules  for  the  Sundays  which  govern  the  weekly  reading  of  the  Old  Testament 
in  the  Autumn  are  complex.  We  have  noted  the  differences  between  the  Services 
set  out  in  the  Breviary  and  those  indicated  by  this  verse,  which  possibly  may  have 
been  framed  according  to  Continental  rather  than  English  customs,  without  at- 
tempting  to  explain  them. 

It  may  be  well  to  mention  that  Aspiciens  is  thc  name  for  the  First  Sunday  in 
Advent,  and  Domine  ne  in  Ira  for  the  First  Sunday  after  the  octave  of  Epiphany.
